items.body:
## Summary

[Section 6.8](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document-01.html#name-client-id-domain-trust) describes heuristic trust decisions (for example, reputation systems or user warning flows) while [Section 6.10](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document-01.html#name-pre-registering-client-id-m) describes exact URL pre-registration of Client ID Metadata Document URLs. The specification does not currently discuss deployment models where authorization servers apply administrator-configured policies based on URL patterns, such as domain allowlists or path-prefix restrictions.

Some enterprise deployments require admitting Client ID Metadata Document URLs based on trusted origins or URL namespaces without requiring exact enumeration of every permitted URL.

## Motivation

### Dynamic-path Client ID Metadata Document URLs

Some deployments generate distinct Client ID Metadata Document URLs per integration or per protected resource while maintaining a common origin and URL structure.

For example, [OpenAI's developer documentation](https://developers.openai.com/apps-sdk/build/auth) describes ChatGPT-originated flows using Client ID Metadata Document URLs of the form:

* `https://chatgpt.com/oauth/github/client.json`
* `https://chatgpt.com/oauth/example/client.json`
* `https://chatgpt.com/oauth/<server>/client.json`

In this model, the authorization server may wish to admit Client ID Metadata Document URLs under a trusted path namespace such as `https://chatgpt.com/oauth/*` without requiring exact pre-registration of every possible URL.

This deployment pattern is not directly addressed by either [Section 6.8](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document-01.html#name-client-id-domain-trust) heuristic trust evaluation or [Section 6.10](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document-01.html#name-pre-registering-client-id-m) exact URL pre-registration.

### Implementation Experience

Related deployment models and implementation mechanisms have appeared in multiple implementations and proposals, including:

* administrative trust configuration for CIMD-enabled deployments
* domain-based trust policy configuration in MCP ecosystem implementations
* [MCP SEP-991](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol/issues/991) discussion of protected-server trust models based on trusted domains or specific clients.

Providing guidance in the specification may improve interoperability and reduce divergence in deployment behavior.

## Proposed Change

Add a subsection under [Section 6.8](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document-01.html#name-client-id-domain-trust) describing pattern-based admission policies for Client ID Metadata Document URLs.

Proposed text:

> Authorization servers MAY apply admission policies to Client ID Metadata Document URLs based on URL patterns rather than requiring exact URL pre-registration as described in [Section 6.10](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document-01.html#name-pre-registering-client-id-m).
>
> Such policies MAY include:
>
> * domain-based allowlists,
> * URL path-prefix matching, or
> * other administrator-configured policy mechanisms.
>
> For example, an authorization server might permit Client ID Metadata Document URLs under a configured namespace such as `https://trusted-client.example.com/oauth/*`.
>
> In enterprise or managed deployments, authorization server implementations SHOULD provide administrators with mechanisms to configure such policies.
>
> Authorization servers SHOULD evaluate these policies before retrieving the referenced metadata document in order to reduce unnecessary outbound requests and limit exposure to SSRF-related attack surfaces described in [Section 6.5](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document-01.html#name-server-side-request-forgery).
>
> Pattern-based admission policies do not replace redirect URI validation requirements. Authorization servers MUST continue validating redirect URIs against the client metadata as described in [Section 4.5](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document-01.html#name-redirect-url-registration).
>
> The syntax and matching semantics of pattern-based policies are outside the scope of this specification.
items.title: Add guidance for pattern-based Client ID Metadata Document URL admission policies

items.body:
For example, if `client_id=https://example.com/oauth/client_id.json`, the AS would `GET https://example.com/oauth/client_id.json?iss=https://example-as.com`.

This allows the client to do a few things:

Progressive rollouts of changes to CIMD, so that blast radius is limited to only certain AS. Making a global change to a client id is bad practice from a production safety point of view, and "random percentage" rollouts may not work if the AS queries the CIMD more than once and gets two different documents.  Of course, `iss` isn't a perfect solution here, but it's easy and better than nothing.

The client could also return AS-specific metadata (as long as it's not secret because `iss` is unvalidated). This could help address certain incompatibilities that may arise in practice where the same values are rejected by some AS but not by others.
items.title: Can AS optionally provide `iss` when fetching client_id?

items.body:
This issue was initially reported by @DavidBuchanan314 in https://github.com/bluesky-social/atproto/issues/3396.

In a federated network, in which hosts are known (as are PDS in the atproto network), the fact that OAuth Server will try to `GET` the client metadata can be used to faking traffic from a bunch of fake IPs, simply by forging authorization requests using the `client_id` as parameter.

For example, by forging the following requests:

- `https://<pds_1>/oauth/authorize?client_id=https://example.com/page_1&...`
- `https://<pds_2>/oauth/authorize?client_id=https://example.com/page_1&...`
- `https://<pds_3>/oauth/authorize?client_id=https://example.com/page_1&...`

The website at `https://example.com/page_1` will see `GET` traffic from the IPs of all those hosts.

Possible mitigations:
- Retrieve the metadata document *after* the user authorized the request (though that could lead to weird UX & DX)
- Add strong constraint on the URI format (eg. `.well-known`, "must end with `.json`", other...)
- ~Recommend OAuth servers to remember the origins of previously failed metadata document retrieval, and prevent more call to be made on these origins~ (redacted: could be abused to cause DoS on legitimate services)
- Other
items.title: Client metadata retrieval can be abused to make server issued requests

In OpenID4VCI, building Interactive Authorization on top of FiPA, we realized that we have three options for the Authorization Challenge Response:
 1. that user interaction is required, either a Presentation, a redirect to web or a custom interaction,
 2. a successful completion of the authorization, as defined in Section 5.2.1 of [@!I-D.ietf-oauth-first-party-apps], or
 3. an error as defined in Section 5.2.2 of [@!I-D.ietf-oauth-first-party-apps], including the additional error codes defined in OpenID4VCI IAE

FiPA defines HTTP Status Codes for both 1. and 3. with 400. I suggest making 1 HTTP 202 or 401 for easier distinguishing.

About req_wl in Requester Context {#requester-context}, especially during replacement, the document says "then this claim will be an array of StringOrURIs representing the different workloads that have requested Txn-Tokens as part of the transaction processing."

Why? Can we change the language to  - claim can be array ? can we leave it to implementation owners?

There are a few reasons why I want to be careful in adding all req_wls involved - 

1. Size - Tx Tokens are going to flow through HTTP headers. In my company, we are careful about size of the token as it flows through HTTP headers. Some web servers block 4KB or more headers and this could be problematic in propagation. If we keep adding all workload identities, then its size will increase. (unpredictable depending on call chain depth)
2. Token context governance - In general, its useful to only add information that could be useful for making authorization decisions, deep down the call graph. In reality, the services deep down call graph are not aware of all services in call path, so they can't really use write access policies using the req_wls anyways as it depends on what call path was taken to reach that service. Also Hyrum's law, that the more you add, the more ways, people will find to make it use of the data in different ways which may not be right.
3. I'd recommend to keep only latest information i.e last req_wl identity and let Token issuer log the exchange details against token identifier in its log to later audit all services where replacement happened.

Also created another issue to cover about having new token id every time there is replacement token generated. https://github.com/oauth-wg/oauth-transaction-tokens/issues/183

Currently, it seems `sub` can be end user identity (if `access token` was used by external endpoint to request Txn-Token from TTS) or it can be External endpoint itself. In former case, external endpoint identity is never captured in the token.

I have a draft for AI agents with Txn-tokens.
https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-oauth-transaction-tokens-for-agents-04.html#name-principal-initiated-flow

In my draft, I had input to TTS as `subject token + access token` received from AI agent at external endpoint (not one of the two inputs but both)

Output we get is: 
​`Txn token {

    Sub: <set to external service> // because TA authenticates subject i.e external endpoint

    Principal : <set to human (from access token)> // new field

    Actor: AI Agent // new field.. this could be ‘act.sub’ but I didn’t use that because ‘act.sub’ could be some internal service that is acting on behalf of external identity.

}`

This is different than Txn token draft because
Txn token draft says external endpoint can pass its self-signed JWT or input access token (w/ token exchange) but I am mandating both.
In my proposal, we don’t lose the external identity.


I do ack that `sub` should be human. If I do that, then I don’t really need Principal. Sub in Txn token should suffice and act.sub will be AI Agent.

### Question 
Basically where am I heading with my question is that can we simply say that this latest draft for Txn-token is good enough to capture `AI Agent + Human identity` (in sub and act.sub) in Txn-token as along as the agent passes an OBO token which has sub and act.sub?

If that is the case, then my draft should simply call out that we need to introduce `act` field and `req_wl` will continue to be the externally visible endpoint

Would love to hear some thoughts on this one from you all?
items.title: Clarification required regarding 'sub' field in Txn-Token

Reviewing the -05 draft, section 5.2.2 identifies the `req_ip` as the IP of the originating user.  However, the bullets identify `req_ip` as belonging to the "end-user or robotic process...".  I find this to be ambiguous about what the `req_ip` represents.  This is further complicated by the fact that the user's IP address may not be available to the call stack because the request has been proxied through one or more devices, obfuscating the user's original IP address.

I have two questions:

1. Can the language around the `req_ip` be tightened up to make it clear that it is either the IP of the end user when issued in exchange for an AT, and it represents the workload's IP when the workload is requesting a replacement txn_token?  The context of a txn_token `req_wl` will make it clear that the `req_ip` is the client (iff `req_wl` is a single element), or the calling workload (iff `req_wl` is > 1 element).
2. Can we add an imperative that the ```req_ip``` for the first txn_token SHOULD NOT be the IP of a proxy or gateway, _e.g._ by using the `X-Forwarded-For` header?

If the authors think these additions are valuable, I can write the PR.

items.body:
## Gap

OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693 §2.2.1) requires the `token_type` response parameter to be `N_A` when the issued token is not used directly as an access token, which is the case for an ID-JAG. This removes the signal that elsewhere in OAuth tells the client which sender-constraint binding (if any) was applied to the issued token. RFC 9449 (DPoP), for example, uses `token_type: "DPoP"` for normal access token responses, but that path is not available for ID-JAGs.

Today the client's only path to detect sender-constraint binding on an ID-JAG is to inspect the ID-JAG itself for an RFC 7800 `cnf` claim. This works for JWS ID-JAGs but fails in two cases:

1. **Encrypted ID-JAGs.** With the JWE-encryption support added in #102, the inner JWS is encrypted to the Resource Authorization Server and is opaque to the client.

2. **Opaque issued tokens generally.** Any future profile that issues opaque tokens via Token Exchange faces the same problem.

The current draft acknowledges this in the DPoP section by recommending the client inspect the ID-JAG for `cnf`, with a caveat (added in #102) that the inspection is impossible when the ID-JAG is encrypted. The result is that a client requesting DPoP binding cannot detect a silent downgrade by the IdP Authorization Server when encryption is in use.

## Why this matters

Without a Token Exchange response-level signal, an IdP Authorization Server that silently fails to apply sender-constraining (by error or by misbehavior) can downgrade the issued ID-JAG without the client noticing. The detection path that exists for unencrypted ID-JAGs (client introspects the JWS) is unavailable for encrypted ID-JAGs, and it never existed for opaque tokens.

This gap is not specific to ID-JAG. Any Token Exchange flow that issues a sender-constrained token where `token_type: "N_A"` is required has the same problem.

## Possible solution

A small extension to RFC 8693 that adds an optional `cnf` parameter to the Token Exchange response. The value reuses the RFC 7800 confirmation structure (`jkt` for DPoP, `x5t#S256` for mTLS, etc.). The authorization server includes it when sender-constraining was applied; the client validates it against the key or certificate it provided in the request. Absence (when binding was expected) is treated as downgrade.

Sketched as an individual draft for working group feedback:

https://mcguinness.github.io/draft-mcguinness-oauth-token-exchange-cnf/draft-mcguinness-oauth-token-exchange-cnf.html

If adopted, the ID-JAG draft could simplify its current DPoP and encryption text by deferring to the response parameter rather than prescribing client-side token introspection.

## Asking for

Feedback on whether a Token Exchange response parameter is the right shape for closing this gap, and whether the sketched draft covers the requirements ID-JAG needs.
items.title: Token Exchange response lacks signal for sender-constraint binding when token_type is "N_A"

items.body:
The current draft generally assumes confidential clients at the Resource Authorization Server (RAS), and the Security Considerations say that this specification `SHOULD` only be supported for confidential clients. The draft also notes in Cross-Domain Client ID Handling that requiring a confidential client at the RAS helps prevent the IdP from delegating access to any valid client at the RAS.

At the same time, the draft now defines proof-of-possession / key-binding for ID-JAG using `cnf` and DPoP. That raises a question about whether the spec should allow an explicit tradeoff here.

**Deployment model to discuss**

- The client is confidential at the IdP.
- The client is public at the RAS, or the RAS otherwise does not require confidential client authentication for this exchange.
- The client includes DPoP in the token exchange to the IdP.
- The IdP issues a key-bound ID-JAG with a `cnf` / `jkt`.
- The client presents DPoP when exchanging the ID-JAG at the RAS.
- The RAS verifies that the DPoP key matches the `cnf` in the ID-JAG.

**Why allow this**

- Credential lifecycle can be centralized at the IdP.
- The client does not need to maintain separate credentials with each RAS.
- This may be useful in ecosystems with many downstream RAS deployments.
- Client ID Metadata Document (CIMD) helps address part of this problem when adopted, but it will not always be available immediately.
- This could make the deployment model possible until CIMD becomes more widely deployed.

**Tradeoff**

This is not equivalent to requiring a confidential client at the RAS.

What is preserved:

- Replay resistance for the ID-JAG, assuming the RAS requires proof-of-possession and validates `cnf` against the proof token.
- Stronger protection than an unconstrained bearer-style exchange.

What is reduced:

- The RAS no longer gets the same client-authentication assurance it gets from a confidential registration at the RAS.
- The anti-client-substitution property is weaker unless the spec explicitly defines how public-client identification is handled in this profile.

**Question**

Should the specification explicitly allow this tradeoff?

Possible direction:

- Keep confidential registration at the RAS as the recommended/default model.
- Allow RAS deployments to accept public clients for ID-JAG exchange when the ID-JAG is key-bound and the proof token presented to the RAS matches the `cnf`.
- Clarify that this does not require any RAS to support public clients.
- A RAS, or the administrator/operator of that RAS, can always decide to require confidential registration instead.
- In that sense, this change would make the model possible, not mandatory, until CIMD is more widely deployed.

If the spec does allow this, it would likely need explicit processing rules for this profile, for example:

- `cnf` in the ID-JAG is required.
- Proof-of-possession at the RAS is required.
- The proof key MUST match the `cnf` in the ID-JAG.
- The RAS SHOULD issue only sender-constrained access tokens in this case.
- The client identification / `client_id` matching rules need to be defined for public clients at the RAS.

The main question is whether the spec should permit this as an optional deployment tradeoff, while still allowing any RAS to require confidential registration.
items.title: Allow public client registration at the Resource Authorization Server when the client is confidential at the IdP and the ID-JAG is key-bound?

Is there anything this spec needs to say about server-provided nonces? 

* [authorization server provided nonce](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9449#name-authorization-server-provid)
* [resource server provided nonce](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9449#name-resource-server-provided-no)

Hi Everyone, 

I've been slowly reviewing the standard document and came across a couple of cases I wanted to bring up:

First:
>    resource:  OPTIONAL - The Resource Identifier (Section 2 of
      [RFC8707]) of the Resource Server (either a single URI or an array
      of URIs).

Can we change this claim description to always be an array of URIs? I understand the recommendation is very nit-picky, although it would be much easier for ID_JAG consumers to handle 'resource' claim validation if it's included.

Second: 
>    client_id:  REQUIRED - The client identifier of the OAuth 2.0
      [RFC6749] client at the Resource Authorization Server that will
      act on behalf of the resource owner (sub).  This identifier MAY be
      different that client identifier of the OAuth 2.0 client
      requesting an ID-JAG from the IdP Section 4.3 of [RFC8693] as it
      represents and independent client relationship to another
      Authorization Server in a different trust domain.  See Section 5
      for additional considerations.

I understand the purpose of this claim and it makes sense, although maintenance of these client_id's can become very cumbersome in large scale deployments, I envision the client_id should be manually set at the AS and there isn't any dynamic relationship between the AS and the Resource Authorization Server. Also perhaps dpop can be used to accomplish the same outcome.

I want to suggest to change the type from "REQUIRED" to "RECOMMENDED". The change would potentially help with the large scale maintenance issues.

Thanks,
Jamshid

In Transaction Tokens, the `aud` claim represents the entire trust domain, which is opposite to OAuth, where it reflects individual resource servers. There is no claim defined that would represent particular workloads as the receivers for the transaction token.

In the absence of the `aud` equivalent having workload-level granularity, how do we implement the "strict audience check" concept from OAuth?

Example: a workload obtains a TraT with audience set to the entire trust domain. Under some circumstances, it might decide to "downscope" the TraT (via replacement request), limiting its "audience" to only selected workloads inside the trust domain, and thus enforcing only a specific request propagation path.

(Credits: Isabella Dix @ Keycloak Dev Day 2026)

items.body:
Problem Statement
A token says what action to perform but not on which specific entity — leaving every service to figure that out independently.

Simple scenario
A loan approval token says action: approveLoan. But there are 50 pending loans. Which one? The loan service has to look up whose loan this is, cross-reference the agent's session, and guess.
More importantly: for shared resources (a document multiple agents can access, a shared account), saying resource: approveloan doesnt justify. The token must say this specific loan, for this specific applicant.

Proposed claim name: action_subject
"tctx": {
"action": "approveLoan",
"action_subject": {
"entity_type": "loan_application",
"entity_id": "loan-8821",
"entity_ref": "[alex.turner@acme.com](mailto:alex.turner@acme.com)"
}
}

A2A examples:
"entity_ref": "agent:financial-analyst-workload"
"entity_ref": "workload:fraud-detection-service-v2"
"entity_ref": "urn:dataset:fraud-training-v3"
"entity_ref": "urn:device:sensor-prod-042"

Taxonomy:
entity_type — what class of thing.
entity_id — unique ID within that class.
entity_ref — how to address or resolve it in the target system.
items.title: action_subject: The specific entity this transaction acts on

items.body:
We have `aud_tenant` defined as an ID-JAG claim as follows:

> aud_tenant:
> OPTIONAL - A JSON string that represents a Resource Authorization Server tenant identifier. This claim is only included when the Resource Authorization Server is multi-tenant and the IdP knows the tenant identifier.

For the case where the IdP and Resource AS do not use tenanted identifiers, and there are multiple copies of the app behind the Resource AS installed in the IdP, this claim is the only thing that can identify the app.

How can a client request a particular app? We didn't want to add `aud_tenant` as a claim to the Token Exchange request. We do have text in the `audience` parameter of token exchange:

> IdP Authorization Servers MAY also support implementation-specific audience values, such as URNs, that identify pre-established trust relationships with Resource Authorization Servers. When such a value is used, the IdP Authorization Server resolves it to the corresponding Resource Authorization Server identifier and issues the ID-JAG with that identifier in the aud claim.

I think two things need to happen:

* We should define a standardized method for referencing `aud_tenant` here
* Update the last part to "...resolves it to the corresponding Resource Authorization Server identifier and issues the ID-JAG with that identifier in the aud claim and aud_tenant"

Thoughts?
items.title: How can a client request a specific `aud_tenant`?

items.body:
A client currently has no way to detect whether an authorization server supports the [RFC 8707 Resource Indicators for OAuth 2.0](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8707.html) extension.  An authorization server that implements support for RFC 8707 would process a requested `resource` and audience-restrict the issued access token if the resource was valid or return an `invalid_target` error code if the requested `resource` is not valid for the authorization server.  If the authorization server doesn't support RFC 8707 it would silently ignore the `resource` parameter and issue an access token to its default audience for the request (e.g  client+scopes requested).  

Since the `access_token` in the token response is opaque to the client, the client has no way to know the value of the issued token's audience.  This is especially problematic when using metadata to dynamically discover an authorization server such as with [OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata  (RFC 9728)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9728.html). 

For example `resource.example` could publish `https://resource.example` as the `resource` identifier but specify `https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/v2/auth` as the authorization server as a phishing attack.  A client would then attempt to obtain an access token from the specified authorization server with the dynamically discovered `resource`  

`https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/v2/auth?client_id=...&scope=...&resource=https://resource.example`. 

If the authorization doesn't support RFC 8707 then it would just process this as a normal authorization request, ignore the invalid resource, and issue a default access token (assuming user consented).   This is the [exact scenario that Model Context Protocol (MCP](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol/pull/284#discussion_r2068009348)) project is vulnerable to which has taken a dependency on OAuth 2.1

While this security risk is explicitly called out in the security considerations of RFC 9728, the interoperability gap still exists for an OAuth 2.1.

> Secure determination of appropriate authorization servers to use with a protected resource for all use cases is out of scope for this specification. This specification assumes that the client has a means of determining appropriate authorization servers to use with a protected resource and that the client is using the correct metadata for each protected resource. Implementers need to be aware that if an inappropriate authorization server is used by the client, an attacker may be able to act as an adversary-in-the-middle proxy to a valid authorization server without it being detected by the authorization server or the client.

If OAuth 2.1 included the [RFC 8707 Resource Indicators for OAuth 2.0](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8707.html) extension, clients could expect an authorization server to process the `resource` or return `invalid_target` error code.  This would help projects like MCP mitigate risks of using metadata based discovery.   **An authorization doesn't need to support `resource` indicators to be complaint.  It just needs to return `invalid_target` if a `resource` is specified.** .  This is small lift for an authorization (support an error code) has a ton a value for dynamic discovery scenarios.

Alternatively, OAuth 2.1 could specify a new token response field for `audience`.  This would push validation to the client to ensure the that issued token was for an audience it wanted and prevent forwarding a token to a resource server with a mismatched audience.   Since audience doesn't need to be 1:1 to a resource's url this is problematic but could be profiled.
items.title: Phishing/Audience Mix-Up Mitigation for Resources

items.body:
Latest couple drafts brought two major changes:
- ABCA can be used as an additional security signal,
- DPoP can be used instead of Client Attestation PoP 

Before those changes, the were some "simple" rules:
- AS had to advertise the authentication method defined by ABCA 
- DPoP was orthogonal and unrelated to ABCA.

As a result, for cases where DPoP was mandated (like for instance in HAIP v1), it was clear that
- the Authorization Server had to issue `access_token`  with `token_type` equal to `DPoP`  (DPoP-bound Access Token)
- the Resource Server had to support [DPoP Authentication Scheme](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9449#name-the-dpop-authentication-sch)

With draft 9,  it is not clear to me, what kind of `access_token` (Bearer or DPoP) the AS is expected to issue when using ABCA as an client authentication method of type `attest_jwt_client_auth`.

In this case, the DPoP is not applicable, so I think that access_token should be issued as bearer not `DPoP`.

On the other hand, there is not reason for not issuing a DPoP Access Token, because both DPoP and Client Attestation PoP are proof of possessing the same key

Can you please clarify on this?
items.title: A Clarification on DPoP Access Token

items.body:
Currently the spec says the client MUST request the `openid offline_access` scopes when exchanging the SAML assertion for refresh token.

It is likely, but not guaranteed, that the SAML assertion that the client has would already include the email address. (SAML can be configured to return opaque values for the `NameId`, and there is no guarantee the IdP would be configured to send an `email` attribute.)

If the SAML assertion did not have the email, you could argue the client should request the email scope because the ID-JAG will be visible to the client and would contain information beyond what is in the SAML assertion.

However, the purpose of including the `email` in the ID-JAG is for the benefit of the Resource AS, when it looks up users by email address from the SAML assertion. This behavior isn't necessarily known by the client, since it's about the relationship between the Resource AS and IdP.

So the question is whether we want to keep the text as is with the `email` claim being optional, or aim for better interoperability by suggesting/requiring that the client request the `email` scope.

Also note that if the IdP includes the `sub_id` property with the SAML NameId values, then the Resource AS likely won't need to rely on the `email` claim at all.
items.title: Should SAML->RT->ID-JAG flow suggest or require the `email` scope?

Currently there is no mention of whether OpenID Connect scopes are allowed or not in the [Token Exchange step](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant-04.html#section-4.3) of the flow.

The text says 

> The space-separated list of scopes at the Resource Server that is being requested.

and OpenID Connect scopes are meant for client consumption, not resource server consumption, so it's kind of implied that they should not be accepted in the Token Exchange request.

Thoughts are welcome about which direction to go, but in either case we should mention that either they are acceptable in the request or they must not be included in the request.

items.body:
# Problem

Section 2.1 of the draft currently says:

> It is RECOMMENDED that the ID-JAG contain an `email` and/or `aud_sub` claim. The Resource Authorization Server MAY use these claims for account resolution or just-in-time (JIT) account creation... Additional Resource Authorization Server specific identity claims MAY be needed for account resolution or JIT account creation.

This language acknowledges the JIT problem but does not solve it. There is no interoperable mechanism for a Resource Authorization Server (RAS) to signal which identity claims it requires, or for a Client to convey that signal back to the IdP so it can include them in the ID-JAG. The result requires out-of-band coordination between every IdP/RAS pair, which undermines the composability goal of the spec.

## Specific failure modes

1. **What claims does the IdP put in the ID-JAG?** The spec provides a fixed optional set (`email`, `aud_sub`) but gives no mechanism for the RAS to express its requirements. IdPs must either over-include claims (privacy risk) or guess conservatively and leave JIT broken.

2. **What claims does the RAS need to JIT?** RAS-specific claims (department, cost center, license tier, custom identifiers) may not be OIDC standard claims. Even for OIDC-defined claims, different RASes need different subsets. There is no way to express this per-RAS, per-deployment requirement today.

3. **How does the IdP know to issue the right claims?** The IdP has no standardized signal from the Client about what the target RAS needs. The Client knows the RAS endpoint (from discovery) but cannot ask the IdP to tailor the ID-JAG for that RAS's JIT requirements.

4. **The UserInfo dead end.** When the RAS receives the ID-JAG it has no Access Token and cannot reach back to the IdP's UserInfo endpoint or any other IdP-hosted endpoint to fetch additional claims. The ID-JAG exchange must succeed or fail on the claims already present in the token. This is not a fixable limitation; it is a structural constraint of the grant flow.

# Proposed Solution

Standardize exactly three things.

## 1. Error code: `insufficient_identity_claims`

If the RAS determines that the identity assertion is cryptographically valid and the grant type is accepted, but the token does not contain sufficient identity claims to perform account resolution or JIT account creation, it SHOULD return an error response per RFC 6749 Section 5.2:

```
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "error": "insufficient_identity_claims",
  "error_description": "The identity assertion is missing required claims for account resolution."
}
```

The name follows the `insufficient_*` pattern established by RFC 9470 (`insufficient_user_authentication`). It signals "valid but not enough", distinguishing this condition from `invalid_grant`, which would indicate the token itself is rejected. 

## 2. Error response parameter: `required_claims`

The error response SHOULD include a `required_claims` parameter: a space-separated list of the claim names the RAS requires, following the same format as `scope` (RFC 6749 Section 3.3):

```json
{
  "error": "insufficient_identity_claims",
  "error_description": "The identity assertion is missing required claims for account resolution.",
  "required_claims": "email department employee_number"
}
```

Space-separated is the right format here. Claim names are JSON member names and cannot contain spaces, so the delimiter is unambiguous. This is consistent with `scope` and avoids the framework-parsing ambiguity of a JSON array in a form-encoded body (cf. RFC 9396 `authorization_details`, which uses JSON because its values are structured objects; claim names are flat tokens and do not warrant that complexity).

`required_claims` is intentionally defined as a flat list of names. Value constraints, type hints, and schema references are deferred pending real deployment experience.

## 3. Token Exchange request extension parameter: `required_claims`

A Client receiving an `insufficient_identity_claims` error MAY retry the Token Exchange request to the IdP Authorization Server, including the `required_claims` parameter with the value carried directly from the RAS error response:

```
POST /oauth2/token
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange
&requested_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:id-jag
&subject_token=<id_token>
&subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:id_token
&audience=https://api.example.com/
&required_claims=email+department+employee_number
```

The symmetric naming (`required_claims` in both the error response and the Token Exchange request) means the Client can pass the value through without transformation. "Required" reflects the RAS's perspective, which is authoritative: these claims are required for the flow to succeed. It does not obligate the IdP to provide all of them; the IdP SHOULD include the requested claims subject to its own policy (consent, availability, privacy controls), and MAY decline to include specific claims.

## End-to-end flow

```
Client → IdP:    Token Exchange → ID-JAG (minimal claims)
Client → RAS:    Token Exchange with ID-JAG
RAS → Client:    400 insufficient_identity_claims
                     required_claims=email department employee_number
Client → IdP:    Token Exchange + required_claims=email department employee_number
IdP → Client:    ID-JAG with additional claims included
Client → RAS:    Token Exchange with enriched ID-JAG
RAS → Client:    200 OK, access_token
```

# Editorial: relax `email` and `aud_sub` to plain OPTIONAL

With `required_claims` providing the negotiation mechanism, the RECOMMENDED status of `email` and `aud_sub` in Section 2.1 should be downgraded to OPTIONAL. These claims become examples of what a RAS might request rather than a standing recommendation that every IdP include them. The existing guidance language should be replaced with a pointer to the `required_claims` mechanism as the interoperable way to express and negotiate claim requirements, and an example end-to-end flow demonstrating the retry pattern.

# Advanced use case: RAS Token Exchange to IdP

For deployments where the identity data needed cannot reasonably be pre-embedded in a signed token (because it is large, sensitive, or needs to be fresher than the ID-JAG allows), the RAS MAY perform its own Token Exchange: presenting the received ID-JAG as the subject token to the IdP's token endpoint and requesting an Access Token scoped to the IdP's identity APIs.

This covers the UserInfo-equivalent pattern without burdening the Client as intermediary, and without embedding what is effectively a profile API response inside the ID-JAG. It should be acknowledged in the spec as a valid deployment pattern with the IdP-side API contract left to a future profile. This keeps the core ID-JAG spec clean and avoids scope creep.

# Optional / future: claim requirements discovery at the RAS

To allow IdPs to import a RAS's claim requirements at onboarding time rather than waiting for a runtime error, the RAS could advertise the claims it needs for JIT provisioning via its Authorization Server metadata (RFC 8414), using a new metadata parameter scoped to this profile (to avoid collision with base OAuth or other profiles).

This is an optimization for IdP onboarding UX, not a correctness requirement. The runtime `insufficient_identity_claims` negotiation works without it. Worth raising for debate; not a blocker for the core proposal.

---

# Questions for the group

1. **Error name:** `insufficient_identity_claims` (cause, RFC 9470 pattern)  or alternative?
2. **IdP acknowledgment:** Should the IdP be required to indicate in the ID-JAG which claims from `required_claims` it was able to include, or is the Client expected to inspect the resulting token before retrying at the RAS?
3. **RAS-to-IdP Token Exchange:** Should the advanced pattern be noted in Security Considerations? The RAS acting as an OAuth client to the IdP has trust and SSRF implications worth calling out even if the pattern itself is out of scope.
items.title: Interoperability gap: JIT provisioning and identity claim negotiation

items.body:
Note - I'm unsure of the best place to discuss this concept but I'm starting the conversation here, due to its potential relationship to this draft.

DPoP as defined in RFC9449 provides a mechanism for sender-constraining tokens issued in OAuth 2.0. By design however the mechanism for sender-constraining of tokens isn't intended to provide wider integrity guarantees over the HTTP message upon which a DPoP proof is attached to. The same problem exists for client attestations.

We've now encountered situations where DPoP (and potentially Client attestations) are (or going to be) used and integrity over the request body of the HTTP message is also desired. This leaves implementations with a couple of possible choices

1. To not have integrity over the request body (beyond what TLS already provides) - This is a difficult argument to make in some of the proposed applications where TLS isn't sufficiently trusted to provide the required integrity
2. To define a seperate mechanism to provide integrity over the request body seperate from DPoP or Client attestations
3. To devise a mechanism whereby a DPoP proof or Client Attestation PoP could also provide integrity over the request body

The remainder of this issue focuses on discussing a proposal for option 3.

HTTP defines a specific header called [Content-Digest](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Digest) which provides a hash/digest over the HTTP message content. In essence, if the value of this header were included inside a DPoP proof / Client Attestation PoP, integrity over the HTTP message content could verified.

An example of a DPoP proof

```
{
  "typ":"dpop+jwt",
  "alg":"ES256",
  "jwk": {
    "kty":"EC",
    "x":"l8tFrhx-34tV3hRICRDY9zCkDlpBhF42UQUfWVAWBFs",
    "y":"9VE4jf_Ok_o64zbTTlcuNJajHmt6v9TDVrU0CdvGRDA",
    "crv":"P-256"
  }
}
.
{
  "jti":"-BwC3ESc6acc2lTc",
  "htm":"POST",
  "htu":"https://server.example.com/token",
  **"htcd": "sha-256=:47DEQpj8HBSa+/TImW+5JCeuQeRkm5NMpJWZG3hSuFU=:",**
  "iat":1562262616
}
```

Note the new `htcd` JWT claim where the value is the value of the Content-Digest HTTP header.

The main advantage I can see to this proposal is that integrity is provided via DPoP without the need for an additional signature over the HTTP message content.

Alternative proposals could involve
1. Providing a seperate signature over the HTTP message using HTTP message signatures - this requires two signatures in the HTTP message
2. Providing a seperate signature over the HTTP message using JWS on the request body - awkward if the request body isn't JSON and also suffers from two signatures in the HTTP message

items.body:
The abstract states:

>    This specification defines an extension to the OAuth 2 protocol as
>    defined in [RFC6749] which enables a Client Instance to include a
>    key-bound attestation in interactions with an Authorization Server **_or_**
>    **_a Resource Server_**.

The Figure and the explanations only address the case of Authorization Servers. The problems for Authorization Servers and Resource Servers are different and, before answering to the question, let us consider some differences.

The document only mentions a recommendation to address the privacy concerns in section 11, and for Authorization Servers only:

>    Client deployments are therefore RECOMMENDED to use different Client
>    Attestation JWTs with different Client Instance Keys across different
>    authorization servers.

A user will usually register to half a dozen of Authorization Servers, but can contract with one or two hundred of Resource Servers. 
The renewal rates of Client Attestation JWTs will be quite different.

The prime argument in the case of Resource Servers is the high renewal rate for Client Attestation JWTs (at least one order of magnitude difference).

The second argument is the fact that the protocol between the Holder and the Verifier can be avoided if a claim about the type of the device and the firmware/software that the device is running is added into digital credentials issued by the Issuer. This scenario is developed in the next issue.

Therefore, I am NOT IN FAVOR of supporting Resource Servers.

items.body:
Section 11 (Privacy considerations) only mentions the case of Client Instance Key in the cnf claim to address the raised privacy issue. 

According to RFC 9334 (RATS Architecture), Section 11 from RFC 9334 states:

> 11.  Privacy Considerations
> 
> (...)
> 
>    In many cases, the whole point of attestation procedures is to
>    provide reliable information about the type of the device and the
>    firmware/software that the device is running.

This means that the* type* of the device and the firmware/software that the device is running should be known to the AS. 

This sentence from Section 11 from RFC 9334 should be copied and pasted into section 11 of this document.

It should be noticed that the protocol will also be applicable if the firmware/software that the device is running is used towards a *single* Authorization Server. In that case, serial numbers can be included into a Client Attestation JWT. This use case supports a nice feature: 
the ability to suspend or revoke a specific Client Attestation JWT.

To this respect the document should include a section addressing the suspension and revocation of a Client Attestation JWT that contains serial numbers.

A digital credential should include one of the two following claims:

-	either a claim about the type of the device and the firmware/software that the device is running, when the Client will be using several Authorization Servers.

-	or a claim about the type of the device and the firmware/software that the device is running, including serial numbers for the device, the firmware and the software that the device is running, only if the Client will be using a single Authorization Server.

If a Client Attestation JWT is used with several Authorization Servers, once the Authorization Server has verified the Client Attestation JWT, it can copy and paste into the digital credential the type of the device and the firmware/software that the device is running.

If a single Client Attestation JWT is used with a single Authorization Server, once the Authorization Server has verified the Client Attestation JWT, it can place into a digital credential the type of the device and the firmware/software that the device is running and omits the serial numbers, if they were present in the Client Attestation JWT. 

This is a transitive trust model.

In this way, the Resource Server can know the type of the device and the firmware/software that the device is running without the need to rely on TLS (HTTPs) to associate that information to the request from the Holder to the Resource Server.

This use case for RSs (or Verifiers) should be explained into an Informative Annex.
items.title: The privacy considerations in section 11 from RFC 9334 should be endorsed

items.body:
Rather than relying on TLS to associate the authentication exchange with the request for a digital credential or for a security token, 
security can be improved by solely relying on the private key which corresponds to the public key placed in the Client Attestation JWT.

The flow (5) is described as follows:

>    (5) The Client Instance generates a Proof of Possession (PoP) with
>        the Client Instance Key.

This flow only supports an authentication service while it can easily accommodate a data origin authentication service.

In the case of a data origin authentication service, a hash value of a former exchange with the Authorisation Server (i.e., the Issuer) can be included into the data that will be signed by the Client Instance Key.

That former exchange can be either a set of claims that the Client Instance requests to be included into a credential that will be issued or a token request.

It is proposed to allow Authorisation Servers to verify, using a single signed message, that the credentials request or the token request indeed originates from a Client instance that supports specific technical characteristics about the type of the device and the firmware/software on which the client instance is running.

In practice, it is proposed to optionally include a hash value of a former request with the Authorisation Server. 

This should be added to the list of claims enumerated in section 5.1.

>    *  req_hash: OPTIONAL.  The req_hash (request hash value) 
>       claim.  Its value is the base64url encoding of the left-most 
>       half of the hash of the octets of the ASCII representation of the
>       request value, where the hash algorithm used is the hash algorithm
>       used in the alg Header Parameter of the ID Token's JOSE Header. 
>       For instance, if the alg is RS256, hash the req_hash value with 
>       SHA-256, then take the left-most 128 bits and base64url-encode 
>       them. The at_hash value is a case-sensitive string.
items.title: The Client Attestation PoP JWT should be able to support a data origin authentication service

items.body:
In [AT Protocol](https://atproto.com/) we've recently published a proposal that takes a similar shape and fills similar use cases to attestation-based client authentication as described in the draft being worked on here.  It can be found here: [0010-client-assertion-backend](https://github.com/bluesky-social/proposals/tree/main/0010-client-assertion-backend).  Once the proposal is finalized, it could end up being widely adopted in the AT Protocol ecosystem, as we have many folks who want to author browser-based clients that are given the security and UX affordances of a confidential client.

We wanted to share our use case and our thinking with the hopes that we may be able to converge on something compatible with the work being done here.

Rather than proposing a new client authentication method, we opted to layer a small mechanism on top of the private_key_jwt method from [RFC 7523](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc7523/).  It's quite limited:
> [If] the `client_assertion` JWT contains a `cnf` claim using the `jkt` method (JWK Thumbprint Confirmation Method) then it MUST be validated by the AS against the public key of the request’s DPoP proof.

The result is DPoP-bound client assertions, which fits neatly with existing DPoP-bound authorization flows, i.e. both authorization code and access token binding as described in [RFC 9449](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9449/).  We considered the need for separate client keys in the client attestation vs. the authorization flow in our proposal, as has been raised in #67 and more recently #74. We do not anticipate any practical issues with using a single PoP key and mechanism, but would be interested to continue getting to the bottom of that question.

On the flip side, we certainly see many benefits to using a single PoP mechanism across these OAuth flows.  We found the following benefits aligning on DPoP and private_key_jwt client authentication:
 - overall the specification becomes much smaller:
   - answers questions around the nonce mechanism, as actively discussed in #101 and #110.
   - supports authorization code binding, as discussed in #56.
   - supports binding the PoP to the attestation used to authenticate, as discussed in #47.
   - answers to the attack surface area when used in conjunction with DPoP-bound access tokens, as discussed in #69.
 - as a result it's more straightforward for client implementers, particularly those who already implement DPoP-bound access tokens, which we believe will continue to rise in popularity. Fewer novel PoP implementations on the client side has its security benefits too.

That's where we're currently at—appreciate the consideration from this group, and the work being done on this draft.
items.title: Similar proposal in AT Protocol: DPoP-bound private_key_jwt client authentication

items.body:
I am very glad to see that the draft is progressing and, in particular, that there is traction to make [things better for DPoP](https://github.com/oauth-wg/draft-ietf-oauth-attestation-based-client-auth/pull/146).

Could I ask you to consider the problem from the perspective of OAuth profiles already built on RFC9449 (DPoP) and RFC7523 (JWT client assertions)?

When both are in use, the AS already processes payloads of the following shape:

```
POST /token.oauth2 HTTP/1.1
Host: as.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
DPoP: eyJ0eXAiOiJkcG9wK2p3dCIsImFsZyI6IkVTMjU2IiwiandrIjp7Imt0eSI6Ik\
  VDIiwieCI6Imw4dEZyaHgtMzR0VjNoUklDUkRZOXpDa0RscEJoRjQyVVFVZldWQVdCR\
  nMiLCJ5IjoiOVZFNGpmX09rX282NHpiVFRsY3VOSmFqSG10NnY5VERWclUwQ2R2R1JE\
  QSIsImNydiI6IlAtMjU2In19.eyJqdGkiOiItQndDM0VTYzZhY2MybFRjIiwiaHRtIj\
  oiUE9TVCIsImh0dSI6Imh0dHBzOi8vc2VydmVyLmV4YW1wbGUuY29tL3Rva2VuIiwia\
  WF0IjoxNTYyMjYyNjE2fQ.2-GxA6T8lP4vfrg8v-FdWP0A0zdrj8igiMLvqRMUvwnQg\
  4PtFLbdLXiOSsX0x7NVY-FNyJK70nfbV37xRZT3Lg

grant_type=authorization_code&
code=n0esc3NRze7LTCu7iYzS6a5acc3f0ogp4&
client_assertion_type=urn%3Aietf%3Aparams%3Aoauth%3A
client-assertion-type%3Ajwt-bearer&
client_assertion=eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6IjIyIn0.\
  eyJpc3Mi[...omitted for brevity...].\
  cC4hiUPo[...omitted for brevity...]
```

These AS already implement DPoP header verification and `client_assertion` JWT validation. In that context, binding the client assertion to the DPoP key can be as simple as embedding the DPoP key thumbprint in the `cnf.jkt` claim of the client assertion. This is essentially a one-line spec change and a [minimal implementation](https://github.com/bluesky-social/atproto/pull/3889/changes#diff-e8a3cdf53808bef6d95a6f8b83c1f35a33d76c369e604f8f47e420c781ae91e0R254-R268).

The current draft introduces a new `token_endpoint_auth_method` and a new `OAuth-Client-Attestation` header with semantics that largely overlap with mechanisms already defined in RFC7523 and RFC9449. The result is an additive design that diverges from existing primitives rather than composing with them.

Starting from those existing RFCs instead would, I believe:

- lower the barrier to adoption, since implementations already handling DPoP and JWT client assertions require minimal changes,
- allow simpler partial adoption (e.g. the DPoP binding alone, without a new auth method),
- reduce the overall complexity added to the OAuth ecosystem.

We may want to consider aligning this text with OAuth 2.1's text: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1#section-4.1.1-28

When comparing the two URIs the authorization server MUST ensure that the two URIs are equal, see [Section 6.2.1](https://rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986#section-6.2.1) of [[RFC3986](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc3986)], Simple String Comparison, for details. The only exception is native apps using a localhost URI: In this case, the authorization server MUST allow variable port numbers as described in [Section 7.3](https://rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8252#section-7.3) of [[RFC8252](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8252)].

items.body:
When a Resource Authorization Server is configured to the enterprise IdP with SAML for SSO, the values currently in the ID-JAG are not able to be mapped to their SAML equivalents.

For example, the Resource AS might recognize a SAML issuer like `https://example.com/exk33qwjcwDda7luK346` and receive SAML NameIds that are a username or email address. An ID-JAG will contain an OIDC issuer URL like `https://tenant123.example.com/` and subject identifiers that are a random string. (there is no guarantee the SAML issuer and OIDC issuer domain names have anything in common.)

When a Resource AS is configured for SAML SSO, what are the options for how it can map the ID-JAG values to the SAML SSO connection? As far as I can tell there are a couple options for the issuer:

* No change to the ID-JAG, require that the customer manually add the OIDC issuer URL into their SAML SSO configuration. This provides the AS the association between the SAML issuer and OIDC issuer.
* Include the SAML issuer in the ID-JAG somewhere.

For the user ID question, the options would be:

* Send whatever value the SAML NameId would have been in the ID-JAG `sub` (this is currently allowed according to [section 3.1](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant-03.html#section-3.1) because it would be "the same as the subject identifier used in an Identity Assertion for the Resource Authorization Server as a Relying Party for Single Sign-On (SSO)")
* Send the SAML NameId as a new claim in the ID-JAG

If we go with adding new claims to the ID-JAG, the question becomes whether these should be SAML-specific claims or something generic, e.g.

* `saml_issuer` and `saml_nameid`
* `alt_issuer` and `alt_sub`

### Minimal Changed Example ID-JAG

```
{
  "typ": "oauth-id-jag+jwt"
}
.
{
  "jti": "9e43f81b64a33f20116179",
  "iss": "https://acme.idp.example",
  "sub": "user@idp.example",                  /* assuming email addresses were sent as SAML NameId */
  "aud": "https://acme.chat.example/",
  "client_id": "f53f191f9311af35",
  "exp": 1311281970,
  "iat": 1311280970,
  "resource": "https://acme.chat.example/api",
  "scope": "chat.read chat.history"
}
.
signature
```

### Example ID-JAG with New Claims

```
{
  "typ": "oauth-id-jag+jwt"
}
.
{
  "jti": "9e43f81b64a33f20116179",
  "iss": "https://acme.idp.example",
  "sub": "U019488227",
  "alt_iss": "https://idp.example/exk33qwjcwDda7luK346",
  "alt_sub": "user@idp.example",
  "aud": "https://acme.chat.example/",
  "client_id": "f53f191f9311af35",
  "exp": 1311281970,
  "iat": 1311280970,
  "resource": "https://acme.chat.example/api",
  "scope": "chat.read chat.history"
}
.
signature
```

items.body: ## Business Case and Demand Today, there is no guidance or pattern for multi-account authorizations in Green Button Connect. While third parties can technically link multiple accounts behind a single subscription ID, Consolidated Edison of New York’s goal is: * **1 subscription ID per account**: To simplify data management. * **Improved performance**: To optimize response times for batch data requests. **Demand:** Customers and third parties (e.g., *Meltek, Runwise, NuEnergen, and Empowered Buildings*) have requested a simpler way to authorize multiple accounts simultaneously for several years. --- ## Conceptual Design (Opt-in, Backward Compatible) The proposal is an opt-in extension of the current OAuth 2.1 authorization code flow. ### 1. Initiation Third parties choose the flow via the `response_type` in the authorization request: * `response_type=code` → Existing single account flow (no change). * `response_type=bulkCode` → New multi-account flow (**opt-in**). ### 2. Authorization Loop In the multi-account flow (`bulkCode`): 1. The user selects one or more accounts to authorize (or “select all”). 2. For each selected account, the data custodian redirects to the third party’s `redirect_uri` with: * A unique `code` for that account. * A `state` parameter containing the original client-supplied state plus metadata. **State Format:** `state = |response_code=bulkCode;current=;total=` > **Example:** If the original state is `123` and there are 2 accounts, the redirect would look like: > `redirect_uri?code=abc&state=123|response_code=bulkCode;current=1;total=2` ### 3. Third-Party Handling * **If `current < total`**: The third party redirects the user to its multi-account authorization continuation page. * *URL Example:* `{base_url}/multi-account-authorization?response_code=bulkCode¤t=1&total=2&status=Success` * **If `current == total`**: The third party redirects the user to its normal post-authorization landing page. * **Interruption**: If the loop is interrupted, all completed authorizations remain valid. --- ## Security Considerations * **State Integrity**: The client must recover the `` and validate it exactly to preserve CSRF protection. * **Metadata Usage**: Appended metadata is **informational only** and must not be used for security-sensitive decisions. * **Implementation**: Clients must implement custom parsing for the state string. Some OIDC libraries requiring an exact string match for `state` may require customization. The [Green Button Alliance](https://www.greenbuttonalliance.org) received the above request from Consolidated Edison of New York. Donald F. Coffin Green Button Alliance Technical Manager dcoffin@greenbuttonalliance.org

items.body:
Imagine a scenario where the user makes a call to the service and requests a transaction, but the actual transaction execution should be deferred or scheduled for later. By that time, the access token will have expired. If the service requests a TraT right away, it will expire as well.

One of the solutions is to use impersonation; when it is time to execute the actual transaction, the service would request a service account token via client credentials grant, then exchange it to the user's access token, which in turn will be used to request a TraT (together with stored request context / details). This adds overhead, and also depends on impersonation support and concrete implementation (e.g. Keycloak provides "[direct naked impersonation](https://www.keycloak.org/securing-apps/token-exchange#_direct_naked_impersonation)").

Can we provide some guidance / recommendations for the above scenario? Is it an option to use a longer-lived credential (e.g. ID token) as `subject_token` in the TraT request?

(Using ID tokens might seem "less secure" compared to access tokens, but according to [OpenID Connect](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html#IDToken) [standards](https://openid.net/specs/fapi-2_0-attacker-model.html#section-2.2), the security requirements for ID tokens are similar to those for access tokens. Additionally, ID token could be even sender-constrained; DPoP doesn't explicitly mention ID tokens, but doesn't prohibit DPoP-binding them.)
items.title: ​​subject_token​ and deferred transactions
Sergio

items.body:
In draft 00 of OAuth SPIFFE Client Authentication, when using Client Authentication with X509-SVID, it requires that the value of the `client_id` request parameter be the SPIFFE ID. However, I believe this requirement should be removed. The reasons are as follows:

* Systems that use the [OpenID Federation 1.0](https://openid.net/specs/openid-federation-1_0.html) specification cannot use OAuth SPIFFE Client Authentication.
* Systems that use the [OAuth Client ID Metadata Document](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document/) specification cannot use OAuth SPIFFE Client Authentication.
* Systems in which client IDs cannot be flexibly changed cannot use OAuth SPIFFE Client Authentication.

The client authentication method defined in RFC 8705 [Section 2.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8705.html#section-2.1) works correctly even if the value of the `tls_client_auth_san_uri` client metadata differs from the client ID.
items.title: Client ID for Client Authentication using X509-SVID

items.body:
> This is missing privacy considerations, please add them. In particular, AS fetching or providing to the end user any URLs dynamically handed over by the client in a CIMD could lead to leaking user usage patterns or information.

This comes from Justin Richer's review (#79), and it is a section we should probably cover. We already have a bunch of security considerations around URLs in CIMDs, but we don't yet have a privacy considerations section. I think this would be an extension of the text in [Dynamic Client Registration](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7591#autoid-23), however, this specifically would not apply:

> Note that clients are forbidden by this specification from creating their own client identifier.

In CIMDs the client does indeed control the document URL and therefore the `client_id`, so could theoretically use those for tracking purposes. I think I've even seen some people attempting this, which lead to some of the restrictions on redirects and other security considerations.

Hi Aaron / Karl / Brian,

Bjørn Baunbæk and Götz Wehberg from the Gimel Foundation here. This is a constructive prior-art notification for any future revision of `draft-ietf-oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant` (WG-adopted 25 August 2025; superseding `draft-parecki-oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant-05` of 2 July 2025).

The Gimel Foundation has published a body of open-core specifications on AI-agent authorization that we believe are directly relevant to - at least - three specific touch-points in the XAA surface as it is likely to evolve. We are filing this as a public-track companion to a direct authors-side note that has been sent off-list to the three of you in parallel.

Three concrete touch-points (not limited to these)
1. `subject_token` shape — PoA Credential as a candidate alongside OIDC ID Token and SAML assertion. Today XAA names the OIDC ID Token and the SAML assertion as the two assertions a client may exchange. The Gimel Power-of-Attorney (PoA) Credential defined in GiFo-RFC 0115 carries a structured mandate (principal, agent, scope, delegation chain, expiry, narrowing rules) and could be carried as a `subject_token` of a third explicitly-named type in a future companion document. This becomes useful the moment XAA needs to describe agent-acting-on-behalf-of-user as distinct from user-with-app, which the "coming soon: secure agent-to-agent delegation" line item in the Okta blueprint will at some point require.

2. Multi-hop scope narrowing — already specified in GiFo-RFC 0115 §3.7. RFC 0115 §3.7 specifies mandatory scope narrowing across multi-hop delegation chains: a sub-agent's credential can only narrow, never broaden, the parent's scope, and this is enforced cryptographically rather than by IdP policy lookup. This is the surface the Okta roadmap names as "secure agent-to-agent delegation" (announced 29 April 2026). When that work begins inside the OAuth WG, RFC 0115 §3.7 is published prior art.

3. Runtime PEP — already specified in GiFo-RFC 0117 §4. RFC 0117 §4 specifies a sixteen-check pre-action enforcement pipeline at the Policy Enforcement Point (scope boundaries, delegation-chain integrity, temporal validity, resource constraints, etc.) with a three-way decision model (PERMIT / DENY / CONSTRAIN — i.e., narrow the action to a subset of what was requested rather than refuse outright). This is the surface the Okta roadmap names as "Agent Gateway." RFC 0117 publishes April 2026; the substantive prior-art anchor for this primitive is also a priority of filed patents.

Requests for a future revision (or a companion document)
A Related Work / Informative Reference entry naming GiFo-RFC 0115 (PoA Credential), GiFo-RFC 0117 (PEP Interface) and beyond as the closest published prior-art surfaces for the three touch-points above, not limited to these.

What this is currently not
- Not an infringement assertion against XAA `-05` or its WG-adopted successor.
- Not a request to change the substantive normative content of XAA itself, which we currently read as architecturally complementary to GAuth.
- A contribution under IETF terms 

All relevant GiFo RFCs are licensed under Apache 2.0 (Specs) or MPL 2.0 (SDKs), both come together with the Legal Terms of the Gimel Foundation. Specs are at `https://github.com/Gimel-Foundation`. Happy to provide section-level pointers or take a call.

Thank you and kind regards!

Bjørn Baunbæk & Götz Wehberg, on behalf of Gimel Foundation

If a value within a credential is a `data:` URI, it would be nice if this could be used in the SVG rendering template. This would allow to represent a credential like you would a physical identity card, and place e.g. the portrait and signature in the credential rendering.

Currently the following text would prevent this from happening:
> Placeholders MUST only be used in the text content of the SVG template and MUST NOT be used in any other part of the SVG template, e.g., in attributes or comments.

To render an image within an svg you need to put the value within the `href` attribute.

Since images are already allowed ("consuming applications MUST ensure that references to external resources (images, etc.) from within the SVG cannot be used to track users or the usage of credentials"), and you must escape content, i don't see any additional security concerns for this.
items.title: Support images as part of SVG rendering?

OAuth 2.1 incorporates RFC 9207's issuer parameter optionally. MCP reveals a rapidly growing use case where mitigating this attack is necessary. See discussion in https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol/issues/1721#issuecomment-3555689564.

items.body:
Potential new Security Consideration - Malicious Clients, Consent Phishing, or other appropriate term:

As service providers adopt stronger user authentication methods, attackers seek additional means to gain access to resources. An attacker may attempt to register an attacker-controlled client with the authorization server, then attempt to trick resource owners into granting the client access to resources through a phishing attack [1][2][3][4]. The access request may not appear malicious to the user as it originates from the legitimate authorization server.

Authorization servers should enforce controls over client registration, as well as controls over the scopes that particular clients are allowed to request. Authorization servers should also allow administrators and/or users to view a list of clients that have been granted access to resources and provide the ability to revoke access.

[1] https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/17/d/pawn-storm-abuses-open-authentication-advanced-social-engineering-attacks.html
[2] https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/ta2552-uses-oauth-access-token-phishing-exploit-read-only-risks
[3] https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2020/07/08/protecting-remote-workforce-application-attacks-consent-phishing/
[4] https://security.googleblog.com/2017/05/protecting-you-against-phishing.html
items.title: Potential new Security Consideration - Malicious Clients (Consent Phishing)

items.body:
Current spec says:

> The client metadata document MUST contain a client_id property whose value MUST compare and match the URL of the document using simple string comparison as defined in [[RFC3986](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-parecki-oauth-client-id-metadata-document-02.html#RFC3986)] Section 6.2.1.

I'm not sure of the reason this text is here, so perhaps there's a good reason?

There's definitely an argument against including `client_id` in the metadata document though. We've seen that implementations of https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8414 often just blindly trust the `issuer` value in the metadata document, without verifying it matches the location they retrieved it from. Omitting `client_id` (by requiring it is not be present and must be ignored if present) from the metadata document sort of completely removes the possibility to do that.

The only downside I can think of is that if the metadata document is somehow getting exposed at multiple urls (https://example.com/client.json and https://www.example.com/client.json for example) then both would end up being valid client ids. I'm not sure if that's bad though?
items.title: Omit `client_id` from client metadata document?

items.body:
Even if remote, there is the possibility that an implementation re-uses the same cryptographic keys for different scopes.

the PoP JWT could be used with the same cryptograhic key attested in more than a single attestation and therefore be replicated for different endpoints/audience

What do you think about getting the `ath` claim inside the DPoP token as requested?

In this way, a DPoP token cannot be replicated when the key that proves possession is the same within different attestations.

Even if DPoP specs defines `ath` in relation to an access token, may we consider that any kind of JWT could represent an access token, in relation of its scope, the flow where it is used and its usage in general?

Then, could we provide a binding of the PoP to a specific attestation where the possession aims to be proved?
items.title: PoP attestation binding

The draft says:

```
The authorization server MUST NOT cache error responses.  The
authorization server also MUST NOT cache documents which are invalid
or malformed.
```

I think there need to be allowances for short-lived negative caching to avoid:

1. Spamming unrelated websites with calls (#30)
2. Exacerbating outages with repeated requests

Maybe leaving it a little vague is ok, something like:

```
The authorization server MUST NOT cache error responses or invalid documents for more than a few minutes.
```

items.body:
## Summary

The CIMD specification does not appear to say how `application_type` should be handled when it is omitted and therefore defaults to `"web"` under [RFC 7591](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7591), but the client uses redirect URI patterns described in [RFC 8252](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8252) for native applications.

This seems relevant because RFC 8252 also says that redirect URI alone is not enough to distinguish client type, and that the client type needs to be recorded during registration so the authorization server can determine how to treat the client.

That leaves some uncertainty around how CIMD is expected to interact with existing OAuth guidance on client type.

## Problem Description

CIMD reuses the OAuth Dynamic Client Registration metadata model from [RFC 7591](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7591). In that model, `application_type` is client metadata, and if it is omitted, the default value is `"web"`.

At the same time, [RFC 8252](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8252) describes redirect URI patterns used by native applications, including loopback redirect URIs. It also says that redirect URI alone is not sufficient to distinguish a public native app from a confidential web client, and that the client type is required to be recorded during client registration.

This creates a question when:

- `application_type` is omitted, so the RFC 7591 default is `"web"`, and
- the client uses loopback redirect URIs associated with native apps in RFC 8252

## Example

Consider a client that:

- omits `application_type`
- uses loopback redirect URIs such as `http://127.0.0.1` or `http://localhost`

Relevant specifications:

- [RFC 7591](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7591)  
  If `application_type` is omitted, the default is `"web"`.

- [RFC 8252](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8252)  
  Loopback redirect URIs are described for native applications, but redirect URI alone is not enough to determine client type, and the client type is required to be recorded during registration.

In that situation, it is not clear how CIMD expects an authorization server to treat the omitted `application_type`:

| Possible reading | Possible result |
| --- | --- |
| Apply the RFC 7591 default strictly | The recorded client type is `"web"` |
| Treat the configuration as incomplete for RFC 8252 purposes | The client metadata is insufficient until client type is explicitly recorded |

CIMD does not currently seem to say how this case should be understood.

## Interoperability Impact

If different implementations handle this differently, the same client configuration may be accepted in one environment and rejected in another.

This appears to have practical relevance in deployed systems, for example:

- [anthropics/claude-code#18251](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/18251)
- [anthropics/claude-code#37747](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/37747)

Possible effects include:

- inconsistent handling of clients that omit `application_type`
- uncertainty about whether the RFC 7591 default is sufficient in RFC 8252 scenarios
- reduced interoperability across implementations

## Question

When `application_type` is omitted and therefore defaults to `"web"` under RFC 7591, but the client uses loopback redirect URIs described in RFC 8252, is that default intended to be sufficient for recording client type, or is explicit client type metadata expected?

## Motivation

Clarifying this would make it easier to understand how CIMD relates to RFC 8252’s requirement that client type be recorded during registration, especially in cases where `application_type` is omitted and the RFC 7591 default may not reflect the intended client type.
items.title: Ambiguity around `application_type` when metadata defaults and usage patterns point to different client types

items.body:
CIMD Section 4.1 client metadata values are those from the DCR Metadata registry but doesn't say what an AS should do when the document contains values the AS doesn't support - for instance a `grant_types` entry like `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code` on an AS that doesn't offer DAG.

Both RFC 7591 and OpenID Connect DCR explicitly permit the AS to either reject or substitute/filter unsupported metadata. RFC 7591 says the AS "MAY reject or replace any of the client's requested metadata values [...] and substitute them with suitable values" and that the client can then "check the values in the response to determine if the registration is sufficient for use."

That last part is key - DCR has a negotiation step. The client sends requested metadata, gets back what the AS actually registered, and decides whether it can work with that. Both behaviors (reject or filter) are fine because the client gets feedback.

CIMD doesn't have this (by design). The client publishes one static document for all ASs. There's no response for the client to inspect. Without guidance in the spec, AS implementers may default to the stricter DCR behavior (reject), either by choice or unknowingly by reusing the DCR client metadata validations, which is at odds with clients having a single general purpose static document.

Example: VS Code publishes `https://vscode.dev/oauth/client-metadata.json` with `grant_types` including `authorization_code`, `refresh_token`, and `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code`. An AS that supports CIMD but not DAG may reject the whole thing, even though `authorization_code` would work fine.

The spec could say that when processing a CIMD, the AS should filter array-valued fields like `grant_types` and `response_types` to the intersection of what the client declares and what the AS supports, and must reject only when that intersection is empty. This is consistent with what DCR already allows - it just makes filtering the expected default for CIMD, which makes sense given the lack of a negotiation step.

But the remaining issue is the potential lack of upfront knowledge. Especially for client metadata related to AS metadata that is defined as optional such as grant_types_supported. Note that I now realize grant_types_supported does have a default specified when omitted.

So I wonder if, combined with the prescribed non-eager reject behaviour, select AS metadata without a default should in addition be made REQUIRED when used in combination with CIMD so that the client knows (or at least can infer) what the resulting metadata likely is that the AS will use. (note I didn't give much thought into scouring each metadata definition for a list just yet)

Refs: https://github.com/panva/node-oidc-provider/issues/1398
items.title: Define AS behavior when CIMD contains unsupported metadata values
